claim: The insect chemosensory repertoires of Odorant Receptors (ORs) and Gustatory Receptors (GRs) together represent one of the largest families of ligand-gated ion channels.
source: The insect chemosensory repertoires of Odorant Receptors (ORs) and Gustatory Receptors (GRs) together represent one of the largest families of ligand-gated ion channels.
evidence: This is a general characterization of the OR/GR family size and function, drawing from established scientific knowledge about these receptor families.

claim: Previous analyses have identified homologous 'Gustatory Receptor-Like' (GRL) proteins across Animalia.
source: Previous analyses have identified homologous 'Gustatory Receptor-Like' (GRL) proteins across Animalia, but the evolutionary origin of this novel class of ion channels is unknown.
evidence: This claim references prior work that identified GRL proteins across animals, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: The evolutionary origin of the GRL class of ion channels is unknown.
source: Previous analyses have identified homologous 'Gustatory Receptor-Like' (GRL) proteins across Animalia, but the evolutionary origin of this novel class of ion channels is unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: Several candidate GRLs were identified in fungi, protists and algae that contain many structural features characteristic of animal GRLs.
source: We describe a survey of unicellular eukaryotic genomes for GRLs, identifying several candidates in fungi, protists and algae that contain many structural features characteristic of animal GRLs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on genomic searches and structural analysis.

claim: The existence of GRL proteins in unicellular eukaryotes provides evidence for homology between GRLs and plant DUF3537 domain proteins.
source: The existence of these proteins in unicellular eukaryotes, together with ab initio protein structure predictions, provide evidence for homology between GRLs and a family of uncharacterized plant proteins containing the DUF3537 domain.
evidence: This claim is based on the discovery of unicellular GRLs combined with computational structure predictions.

claim: Ab initio protein structure predictions provide evidence for homology between GRLs and plant DUF3537 domain proteins.
source: The existence of these proteins in unicellular eukaryotes, together with ab initio protein structure predictions, provide evidence for homology between GRLs and a family of uncharacterized plant proteins containing the DUF3537 domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The GRL protein superfamily originated in the last common eukaryotic ancestor.
source: Together, our analyses suggest an origin of this protein superfamily in the last common eukaryotic ancestor.
evidence: This is the main evolutionary conclusion of the study, inferred from the phylogenetic distribution and structural analysis of GRLs.

claim: The insect chemosensory receptor superfamily forms a critical molecular interface between diverse chemical signals in the environment and neural activity patterns that evoke behavioral responses.
source: The insect chemosensory receptor superfamily, comprising Odorant Receptors (ORs) and Gustatory Receptors (GRs), forms a critical molecular interface between diverse chemical signals in the environment and neural activity patterns that evoke behavioral responses (Benton, 2015; Joseph and Carlson, 2015; Robertson, 2019; Rytz et al., 2013; van Giesen and Garrity, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Most insect genomes encode dozens to hundreds of different, often species-specific, ORs and/or GRs.
source: Most insect genomes encode dozens to hundreds of different, often species-specific, ORs and/or GRs.
evidence: This is a general observation about insect OR/GR repertoire sizes based on established genomic knowledge.

claim: The vast majority of insect ORs and GRs are likely to be expressed in, and define the chemical response properties of, distinct subpopulations of peripheral sensory neurons.
source: Detailed analyses, in particular in Drosophila melanogaster, indicate that the vast majority of these are likely to be expressed in, and define the chemical response properties of, distinct subpopulations of peripheral sensory neurons (Chen and Dahanukar, 2020; Joseph and Carlson, 2015; Scott, 2018; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by detailed analyses cited from Drosophila studies.

claim: Insect ORs derived from an ancestral GR.
source: Insect ORs and GRs – the former having derived from an ancestral GR (Robertson, 2019; Robertson et al., 2003) – contain seven transmembrane (TM) domains (Clyne et al., 2000; Clyne et al., 1999; Scott et al., 2001; Vosshall et al., 1999).
evidence: This evolutionary relationship is supported by citations to Robertson's work.

claim: Insect ORs and GRs contain seven transmembrane (TM) domains.
source: Insect ORs and GRs – the former having derived from an ancestral GR (Robertson, 2019; Robertson et al., 2003) – contain seven transmembrane (TM) domains (Clyne et al., 2000; Clyne et al., 1999; Scott et al., 2001; Vosshall et al., 1999).
evidence: This structural feature is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Vertebrate olfactory and taste receptors belong to the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) superfamily of seven TM domain proteins.
source: In contrast to vertebrate olfactory and taste receptors, which belong to the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) superfamily of seven TM domain proteins (Glezer and Malnic, 2019; Yarmolinsky et al., 2009), insect ORs and GRs have the opposite topology, with an intracellular N-terminus (Benton et al., 2006; Lundin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison to vertebrate receptors supported by citations.

claim: Insect ORs and GRs have the opposite topology to vertebrate olfactory and taste receptors, with an intracellular N-terminus.
source: In contrast to vertebrate olfactory and taste receptors, which belong to the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) superfamily of seven TM domain proteins (Glezer and Malnic, 2019; Yarmolinsky et al., 2009), insect ORs and GRs have the opposite topology, with an intracellular N-terminus (Benton et al., 2006; Lundin et al., 2007).
evidence: This structural difference is supported by citations to studies that determined the topology.

claim: Insect ORs and GRs form ligand-gated ion channels.
source: Functional analyses of these proteins in heterologous expression systems indicate that they form ligand-gated ion channels (Butterwick et al., 2018; Sato et al., 2008; Sato et al., 2011; Wicher et al., 2008).
evidence: This functional characterization is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Insect ORs assemble into heteromeric (probably tetrameric) complexes likely composed of two subunits each of a tuning OR and a universal co-receptor ORCO.
source: Insect ORs assemble into heteromeric (probably tetrameric) complexes likely composed of two subunits each of a tuning OR, which recognizes odor ligands, and a universal co-receptor, ORCO, which is critical for complex assembly, subcellular trafficking, and – together with the tuning OR – forms the ion conduction pore (Benton et al., 2006; Butterwick et al., 2018; Larsson et al., 2004; Sato et al., 2008; Wicher et al., 2008).
evidence: This structural and functional description is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ORCO is critical for complex assembly, subcellular trafficking, and forms the ion conduction pore together with the tuning OR.
source: Insect ORs assemble into heteromeric (probably tetrameric) complexes likely composed of two subunits each of a tuning OR, which recognizes odor ligands, and a universal co-receptor, ORCO, which is critical for complex assembly, subcellular trafficking, and – together with the tuning OR – forms the ion conduction pore (Benton et al., 2006; Butterwick et al., 2018; Larsson et al., 2004; Sato et al., 2008; Wicher et al., 2008).
evidence: This functional role of ORCO is supported by multiple citations.

claim: GRs are likely to function in multimeric complexes of one or more different subunits.
source: GRs are less well-characterized but are also likely to function in multimeric complexes of one or more different subunits (Joseph and Carlson, 2015; Scott, 2018).
evidence: This claim about GR assembly is supported by citations.

claim: A cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of an ORCO homotetramer demonstrated that this receptor adopts a novel fold unrelated to any known family of ion channels.
source: A cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of an ORCO homotetramer (Butterwick et al., 2018) – which can conduct ions itself upon stimulation with artificial ligands (Jones et al., 2011) – demonstrated that this receptor adopts a novel fold unrelated to any known family of ion channels.
evidence: This structural finding is supported by citation to the cryo-EM study.

claim: ORCO can conduct ions itself upon stimulation with artificial ligands.
source: A cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of an ORCO homotetramer (Butterwick et al., 2018) – which can conduct ions itself upon stimulation with artificial ligands (Jones et al., 2011) – demonstrated that this receptor adopts a novel fold unrelated to any known family of ion channels.
evidence: This functional property is supported by citation.

claim: Analysis of amino acid conservation across the OR repertoire and de novo structure predictions suggest that the ORCO fold is globally similar for all ORs and potentially GRs.
source: Analysis of amino acid conservation across the OR repertoire (Butterwick et al., 2018) and de novo structure predictions of tuning ORs, guided by patterns of amino acid co-evolution (Hopf et al., 2015), suggest that this fold is globally similar for all ORs (and potentially GRs).
evidence: This claim is based on computational analyses cited in the text.

claim: The most extensive comparative genomic analyses of ORs have focused on Insecta, tracing the origins of the OR family from the ancestral insect GRs.
source: The most extensive comparative genomic analyses have focused on Insecta, tracing the origins of the OR family from the ancestral insect GRs (Brand et al., 2018; Missbach et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement about prior comparative genomic work is supported by citations.

claim: Surveys for GR-like (GRL) proteins beyond insects have identified members of this family across Protostomia (including in Annelida, Nematoda, and Mollusca) as well as in a limited number of Deuterostomia (including Echinodermata and Hemichordata, but not Chordata).
source: Surveys for GR-like (GRL) proteins beyond insects have identified members of this family across Protostomia (including in Annelida, Nematoda, and Mollusca) as well as in a limited number of Deuterostomia (including Echinodermata and Hemichordata, but not Chordata) (Eyun et al., 2017; Robertson, 2015; Saina et al., 2015).
evidence: This phylogenetic distribution is supported by citations to prior surveys.

claim: Several non-bilaterian animals have recognizable GRLs, including Cnidaria and Placozoa.
source: Several non-bilaterian animals have recognizable GRLs, including Cnidaria and Placozoa (Eyun et al., 2017; Nordstrom et al., 2011; Robertson, 2015; Saina et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Two homologs in Caenorhabditis elegans (LITE-1 and GUR-3) function in light detection.
source: For example, two homologs in Caenorhabditis elegans (LITE-1 and GUR-3) function in light detection (Edwards et al., 2008), either as a photoreceptor (Gong et al., 2016), or indirectly through recognition of cellular chemical products produced upon light exposure (Bhatla and Horvitz, 2015).
evidence: This functional role is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: LITE-1 functions as a photoreceptor in C. elegans.
source: For example, two homologs in Caenorhabditis elegans (LITE-1 and GUR-3) function in light detection (Edwards et al., 2008), either as a photoreceptor (Gong et al., 2016), or indirectly through recognition of cellular chemical products produced upon light exposure (Bhatla and Horvitz, 2015).
evidence: This specific mechanism is supported by citation.

claim: GUR-3 functions indirectly in light detection through recognition of cellular chemical products produced upon light exposure.
source: For example, two homologs in Caenorhabditis elegans (LITE-1 and GUR-3) function in light detection (Edwards et al., 2008), either as a photoreceptor (Gong et al., 2016), or indirectly through recognition of cellular chemical products produced upon light exposure (Bhatla and Horvitz, 2015).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation.

claim: Isoforms of the D. melanogaster LITE-1 ortholog, GR28b, have roles in thermosensation and light-sensing.
source: (Isoforms of the D. melanogaster LITE-1 ortholog, GR28b, also have other sensory roles, notably in thermosensation and light-sensing (Ni et al., 2013; Xiang et al., 2010).)
evidence: These functional roles are supported by citations.

claim: Another C. elegans homolog functions in motoneurons to control egg-laying.
source: Another C. elegans homolog functions in motoneurons to control egg-laying (Moresco and Koelle, 2004).
evidence: This functional role is supported by citation.

claim: GRLs in the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis and the purple sea urchin, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus are expressed early during development.
source: GRLs in the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis and the purple sea urchin, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus are expressed early during development (Saina et al., 2015), and one of the N. vectensis proteins may have a role in apical body patterning (Saina et al., 2015).
evidence: This expression pattern is supported by citation.

claim: One of the N. vectensis GRL proteins may have a role in apical body patterning.
source: GRLs in the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis and the purple sea urchin, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus are expressed early during development (Saina et al., 2015), and one of the N. vectensis proteins may have a role in apical body patterning (Saina et al., 2015).
evidence: This potential role is supported by citation and is stated as speculative ('may have').

claim: The GRL family of ion channels represents one of the largest and most functionally diverse in nature.
source: Although this family of established (or presumed) ion channels represents one of the largest and most functionally diverse in nature, its evolutionary origin remains unknown.
evidence: This characterization is based on the accumulated knowledge about GRL diversity and function.

claim: Potential homology between GRLs and plant DUF3537 proteins was previously suggested based upon their predicted seven TM domains and intracellular N-termini.
source: We previously suggested potential homology between GRLs and a family of uncharacterized plant proteins containing the Domain of Unknown Function 3537 (DUF3537), based upon their predicted seven TM domains and intracellular N-termini (Benton, 2015).
evidence: This is a reference to a prior hypothesis by the authors.

claim: The proposal of homology between GRLs and DUF3537 proteins was questioned because DUF3537 proteins lack other features that characterize animal GRLs, such as a motif in TM7 and conserved introns near the 3' end of the corresponding gene.
source: However, this proposal was questioned (Robertson, 2019) because DUF3537 proteins lack other features that characterize animal GRLs, such as a motif in TM7 and conserved introns near the 3' end of the corresponding gene (Robertson, 2015; Robertson, 2019; Saina et al., 2015).
evidence: This criticism is supported by citations to Robertson's work.

claim: 17 candidate GRL sequences were identified from Fungi, Protista and unicellular Plantae.
source: These analyses identified 17 sequences from Fungi, Protista and unicellular Plantae (Table 1 and Figure 1), described in more detail below.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on database searches.

claim: HMMs of all new candidate sequences display significant similarity to those of multiple animal and/or plant proteins.
source: Importantly, HMMs of all new candidate sequences display significant similarity to those of multiple animal and/or plant proteins.
evidence: This is based on HMM alignment analysis performed in the study.

claim: Some candidate GRLs clustered more closely with animal sequences, while others displayed similar probabilities with both animal and plant proteins.
source: Some candidates clustered more closely with the animal sequences, while others displayed similar probabilities with both animal and plant proteins, an observation consistent with phylogenetic analyses presented below.
evidence: This observation is based on HMM similarity analysis.

claim: The TM7 motif in animal GRLs is (T/S)Yhhhhh(Q/K/E)(F/L/M), where h denotes a hydrophobic amino acid.
source: We also examined the candidate homologs for the only known primary sequence feature of animal GRLs, a short motif located in the C-terminal half of TM7: (T/S)Yhhhhh(Q/K/E)(F/L/M), where h denotes a hydrophobic amino acid (Robertson, 2015).
evidence: This motif definition is supported by citation.

claim: Many insect tuning ORs and some GRs/GRLs have divergent amino acids at some or all four positions of the TM7 motif.
source: This motif is diagnostic, but not definitive: many insect tuning ORs (as well as some GRs/GRLs) have divergent amino acids at some or all four positions (Robertson, 2019; Scott et al., 2001).
evidence: This observation about motif variability is supported by citations.

claim: The TY residues of the TM7 motif form part of the interaction interface between subunits in ORCO.
source: Structural and functional analyses of a subset of residues of this motif in ORCO indicates that the TY residues form part of the interaction interface between subunits (Figure 2A), and that their mutation is detrimental to function in some, but not all, combinations of subunits (Butterwick et al., 2018; Nakagawa et al., 2012).
evidence: This structural role is supported by citations to structural and functional studies.

claim: Mutation of the TY residues in the TM7 motif is detrimental to function in some, but not all, combinations of subunits.
source: Structural and functional analyses of a subset of residues of this motif in ORCO indicates that the TY residues form part of the interaction interface between subunits (Figure 2A), and that their mutation is detrimental to function in some, but not all, combinations of subunits (Butterwick et al., 2018; Nakagawa et al., 2012).
evidence: This functional consequence is supported by citations.

claim: The terminal L residue of the TM7 motif is part of the channel gate.
source: The terminal L residue of the motif is part of the channel gate (Figure 2A), and its mutation alters ion permeation selectivity (Butterwick et al., 2018).
evidence: This structural role is supported by citation and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Mutation of the terminal L residue of the TM7 motif alters ion permeation selectivity.
source: The terminal L residue of the motif is part of the channel gate (Figure 2A), and its mutation alters ion permeation selectivity (Butterwick et al., 2018).
evidence: This functional consequence is supported by citation.

claim: Divergence from the GRL motif in a given protein could be compatible with a conserved function as an ion channel, albeit with different complex assembly and biophysical properties.
source: These observations suggest that divergence from the GRL motif in a given protein could be compatible with a conserved function as an ion channel, albeit with different complex assembly and biophysical properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed variability in the motif and its functional consequences.

claim: A single candidate GRL was identified in Spizellomyces punctatus.
source: A single candidate GRL was identified in two fungi, Spizellomyces punctatus (Russ et al., 2016) and Spizellomyces palustris (van de Vossenberg et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the database searches performed in the study.

claim: A single candidate GRL was identified in Spizellomyces palustris.
source: A single candidate GRL was identified in two fungi, Spizellomyces punctatus (Russ et al., 2016) and Spizellomyces palustris (van de Vossenberg et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the database searches performed in the study.

claim: The fungal GRL proteins exhibit the secondary structural features of GRLs.
source: The fungal proteins exhibit the secondary structural features of GRLs (Figure 1), but only one of the four positions of the TM7 motif is conserved (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on structural predictions shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the fungal GRLs, only one of the four positions of the TM7 motif is conserved.
source: The fungal proteins exhibit the secondary structural features of GRLs (Figure 1), but only one of the four positions of the TM7 motif is conserved (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Spizellomyces punctatus and Spizellomyces palustris are chytrids, an early diverging lineage of fungi that retains some features of the last common opisthokont ancestor of animals and fungi.
source: Both of these species are chytrids, an early diverging lineage of fungi that retains some features of the last common opisthokont ancestor of animals and fungi (Medina and Buchler, 2020).
evidence: This phylogenetic characterization is supported by citation.

claim: Chytrids reproduce via zoospores, which use a motile cilium to swim or crawl.
source: Chytrids have diverse lifestyles, but are notable for their reproduction via zoospores, which use a motile cilium to swim or crawl.
evidence: This is general biological knowledge about chytrids.

claim: Thecamonas trahens has six candidate GRL proteins.
source: The marine gliding zooflagellate Thecamonas trahens (Cavalier-Smith and Chao, 2010; Howe et al., 2020) has six candidate proteins.
evidence: This is a finding from the database searches.

claim: Thecamonas trahens GRL proteins have up to three conserved residues of the TM7 motif.
source: Beyond secondary structural similarity (Figure 1), the proteins have up to three conserved residues of the TM7 motif (if counting a Y→F substitution in the second position as conservative, as observed in some animal GRLs (e.g., SpurGRL1)) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Vitrella brassicaformis has six GRLs.
source: The chromerid Vitrella brassicaformis (Woo et al., 2015), a free-living, non-parasitic photosynthetic protist, also has six GRLs, most of which have two conserved positions within the TM7 motif.
evidence: This is a finding from the database searches.

claim: Most Vitrella brassicaformis GRLs have two conserved positions within the TM7 motif.
source: The chromerid Vitrella brassicaformis (Woo et al., 2015), a free-living, non-parasitic photosynthetic protist, also has six GRLs, most of which have two conserved positions within the TM7 motif.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Protostelium aurantium var. fungivorum has a single GRL.
source: Finally, the amoebozoan Protostelium aurantium var. fungivorum (Hillmann et al., 2018), has a single GRL.
evidence: This is a finding from the database searches.

claim: DUF3537 domain proteins are widely (and possibly universally) encoded in higher plant genomes, typically comprising small families of 4–12 members.
source: DUF3537 domain proteins are widely (and possibly universally) encoded in higher plant genomes, typically comprising small families of 4–12 members (Benton, 2015).
evidence: This is a general observation about DUF3537 distribution supported by citation.

claim: Single DUF3537 proteins were found in the marine microalgae Chloropicon primus and Micromonas pusilla.
source: Single proteins were also found in unicellular plants ('green algae'), including the marine microalgae Chloropicon primus (Lemieux et al., 2019) and Micromonas pusilla (van Baren et al., 2016; Worden et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from the database searches.

claim: The TM7 motif is largely unrecognizable in plant DUF3537 sequences.
source: As for higher plant sequences, the TM7 motif is largely unrecognizable.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The relationship between DUF3537 proteins and the GRL superfamily may have been overlooked earlier because protein alignments are impeded by the longer length of several intracellular loops of the plant proteins.
source: The relationship between DUF3537 proteins and the GRL superfamily may have been overlooked earlier because protein alignments are impeded by the longer length of several intracellular loops (IL) of the plant proteins, notably IL3 in all DUF3537 proteins, and IL2 in the green algal proteins (~200 residues in the C. primus homolog) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference about why homology was not recognized earlier, based on structural features shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ORCO is distinguished from other insect ORs and GRs by an additional ~60–70 amino acids in IL2.
source: We note that ORCO is also distinguished from other insect ORs and GRs by an additional ~60–70 amino acids in IL2 (Benton et al., 2006), a region that contributes to channel regulation (Bahk and Jones, 2016; Mukunda et al., 2014).
evidence: This structural feature and its functional role are supported by citations.

claim: The IL2 region in ORCO contributes to channel regulation.
source: We note that ORCO is also distinguished from other insect ORs and GRs by an additional ~60–70 amino acids in IL2 (Benton et al., 2006), a region that contributes to channel regulation (Bahk and Jones, 2016; Mukunda et al., 2014).
evidence: This functional role is supported by citations.

claim: Candidate GRLs are extremely divergent in primary sequence, with pairwise alignments revealing as little as 10% amino acid identity.
source: The candidate GRLs are extremely divergent in primary sequence: pairwise alignment of the new proposed family members, together with representative animal and plant proteins, reveal as little as 10% amino acid identity.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis performed in the study.

claim: Insect OR families have an average of only ~20% amino acid identity.
source: While this divergence does not preclude their definition as homologs – insect OR families themselves have an average of only ~20% amino acid identity (Butterwick et al., 2018) – it makes it difficult to infer homology from sequence alone, and hinders confident multiprotein alignment.
evidence: This comparison is supported by citation.

claim: There are no universally conserved residues in GRLs beyond the hydrophobic regions predicted to be TM domains.
source: Indeed, an alignment of these 17 sequences, together with selected animal GRLs and plant DUF3537 proteins highlights the absence of any universally conserved residues, beyond the hydrophobic regions predicted to be TM domains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the multiple sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: TM regions are most confidently aligned in the C-terminal halves of GRL proteins, with substantial variation in loop lengths fragmenting the N-terminal halves.
source: These TM regions are most confidently aligned in the C-terminal halves of the proteins, with substantial variation in loop lengths fragmenting the N-terminal halves (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is based on the alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The pattern of conservation along the protein length (more conserved C-terminal half) is characteristic of insect OR/GR families.
source: This pattern of conservation along the protein length is characteristic of insect OR/GR families (Robertson, 2015; Robertson, 2019; Saina et al., 2015), which might reflect the role of the N-terminal half in ligand-recognition (and commensurate higher divergence between proteins) and the C-terminal half in mediating subunit interactions and forming the ion channel pore (Butterwick et al., 2018).
evidence: This pattern is supported by citations and an inference about functional significance.

claim: The N-terminal half of GRLs may be involved in ligand-recognition.
source: This pattern of conservation along the protein length is characteristic of insect OR/GR families (Robertson, 2015; Robertson, 2019; Saina et al., 2015), which might reflect the role of the N-terminal half in ligand-recognition (and commensurate higher divergence between proteins) and the C-terminal half in mediating subunit interactions and forming the ion channel pore (Butterwick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about functional roles based on conservation patterns.

claim: The C-terminal half of GRLs mediates subunit interactions and forms the ion channel pore.
source: This pattern of conservation along the protein length is characteristic of insect OR/GR families (Robertson, 2015; Robertson, 2019; Saina et al., 2015), which might reflect the role of the N-terminal half in ligand-recognition (and commensurate higher divergence between proteins) and the C-terminal half in mediating subunit interactions and forming the ion channel pore (Butterwick et al., 2018).
evidence: This functional role is supported by citation to the ORCO structure study.

claim: Animal and plant/algal GRL proteins form distinct clades in the phylogenetic tree.
source: As expected, the animal and plant/algal proteins form distinct clades.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The sets of GRLs of V. brassicaformis and T. trahens segregate into two lineages, one of which is more closely related to animal GRLs.
source: The sets of GRLs of V. brassicaformis and T. trahens GRLs segregate into two lineages, one of which (comprising VbraGRL1/2 and TtraGRL1/2/3) is more closely related to animal GRLs, while the others are more distantly related; this distinction matches observations from the alignments of HMMs derived from these sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic tree in Figure 2C and HMM alignments in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Low branch support does not allow for a confident placement of the fungal GRLs in the phylogenetic tree.
source: Low branch support does not allow for a confident placement of the fungal GRLs; they could group with either of the two protist lineages.
evidence: This is an assessment of the phylogenetic analysis results.

claim: Most query sequences successfully seeded a multisequence alignment to permit extraction of co-evolutionary couplings, generation of inter-residue contact maps and prediction of three-dimensional models using trRosetta.
source: Most query sequences successfully seeded a multisequence alignment to permit extraction of co-evolutionary couplings, generation of inter-residue contact maps and prediction of three-dimensional models (Figure 3A–B, Supplementary file 7; full outputs of modeling are provided in the Dryad repository doi:10.5061/dryad.s7h44j15f).
evidence: This describes the computational modeling results.

claim: The contact maps predicted consistent patterns of anti-parallel packing of TM helices across GRLs and DUF3537 proteins.
source: The contact maps predicted consistent patterns of anti-parallel packing of TM helices (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on the contact maps shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The top-predicted models of GRLs and DUF3537 proteins were qualitatively similar to the AbakORCO cryo-EM structure, particularly in the transmembrane core.
source: Concordantly, the top-predicted models were qualitatively similar to the AbakORCO cryo-EM structure (Figure 3B), particularly in the transmembrane core of these models (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of predicted models shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The consistent helical packing of GRLs and DUF3537 proteins is fundamentally different to the Homo sapiens Adiponectin Receptor 1 (HsapAdipoR1).
source: Importantly, the consistent helical packing of GRLs and DUF3537 proteins is fundamentally different to an unrelated seven TM protein, the Homo sapiens Adiponectin Receptor 1 (HsapAdipoR1), which – despite sharing the same membrane orientation as GRLs – displays an arrangement of helices that is convergent with that of GPCRs (Hopf et al., 2015; Vasiliauskaité-Brooks et al., 2017; Figure 3B).
evidence: This comparison is based on structural models and supported by citations.

claim: HsapAdipoR1 displays an arrangement of helices that is convergent with that of GPCRs.
source: Importantly, the consistent helical packing of GRLs and DUF3537 proteins is fundamentally different to an unrelated seven TM protein, the Homo sapiens Adiponectin Receptor 1 (HsapAdipoR1), which – despite sharing the same membrane orientation as GRLs – displays an arrangement of helices that is convergent with that of GPCRs (Hopf et al., 2015; Vasiliauskaité-Brooks et al., 2017; Figure 3B).
evidence: This structural similarity is supported by citations.

claim: Dali searches of the Protein Data Bank with predicted GRL and DUF3537 models identified the AbakORCO cryo-EM structure as the top hit for essentially all models.
source: We confirmed these observations first by heuristic searches of the Protein Data Bank (PDB) with Dali (Holm and Rosenström, 2010): strikingly, essentially all models identified the AbakORCO cryo-EM structure as the top hit (Supplementary file 7; outputs of Dali searches are provided in the Dryad repository doi:10.5061/dryad.s7h44j15f).
evidence: This is based on Dali search results.

claim: Quantitative pairwise comparisons of selected structures using both Dali and TM-align indicated that all family members are likely to adopt the same global protein fold.
source: Second, quantitative pairwise comparisons of selected structures using both Dali and TM-align (Zhang and Skolnick, 2005) indicated that all family members are likely to adopt the same global protein fold, while displaying only random structural similarity to our negative control HsapAdipoR1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: GRL and DUF3537 proteins display only random structural similarity to HsapAdipoR1.
source: Second, quantitative pairwise comparisons of selected structures using both Dali and TM-align (Zhang and Skolnick, 2005) indicated that all family members are likely to adopt the same global protein fold, while displaying only random structural similarity to our negative control HsapAdipoR1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: RaptorX models of unicellular eukaryotic GRLs and plant DUF3537 proteins also identified AbakORCO as the top hit in Dali PDB searches.
source: We extended this analysis by generating protein models with an independent algorithm, RaptorX (Källberg et al., 2012), and assessing these using Dali PDB searches. Where reliable models were generated (excluding those resulting from multisequence alignments consisting of only a few proteins), AbakORCO was again repeatedly identified as the top hit for animal and unicellular eukaryotic GRLs and plant DUF3537 proteins (Supplementary file 7; full outputs of modeling are provided in the Dryad repository doi:10.5061/dryad.s7h44j15f).
evidence: This is based on RaptorX modeling and Dali search results.

claim: The trRosetta and RaptorX models of unicellular eukaryotic GRLs derive from multisequence alignments containing large numbers of animal proteins.
source: It is important to recognize that the trRosetta and RaptorX models of unicellular eukaryotic GRLs derive from multisequence alignments containing large numbers of animal proteins.
evidence: This is a methodological observation about the modeling process.

claim: The models of plant DUF3537 proteins used information extracted from alignments of only other DUF3537 family members.
source: Importantly, the models of the plant proteins used information extracted from alignments of only other DUF3537 family members, presumably because the primary sequence similarity of members of the more divergent plant and animal proteins is below the threshold of both trRosetta and RaptorX algorithms.
evidence: This is a methodological observation about the modeling process.

claim: The independently-generated plant protein models are similar to AbakORCO.
source: The observation that the independently-generated plant protein models are also similar to AbakORCO argues that, despite their high sequence divergence, animal and protist GRLs and plant DUF3537 proteins all adopt a common three-dimensional architecture.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison of the models.

claim: Despite high sequence divergence, animal and protist GRLs and plant DUF3537 proteins all adopt a common three-dimensional architecture.
source: The observation that the independently-generated plant protein models are also similar to AbakORCO argues that, despite their high sequence divergence, animal and protist GRLs and plant DUF3537 proteins all adopt a common three-dimensional architecture.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural modeling results.

claim: Primary, secondary and tertiary structural analyses together support the hypothesis that animal ORs/GRs/GRLs, newly-recognized unicellular eukaryotic GRLs, and plant DUF3537 proteins are homologous.
source: Nevertheless, our primary, secondary and tertiary structural analyses together support the hypothesis that animal ORs/GRs/GRLs, newly-recognized unicellular eukaryotic GRLs, and plant DUF3537 proteins are homologous.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The extremely sparse phylogenetic distribution of GRL genes in unicellular eukaryotes might be explained by independent losses in many lineages and/or divergence beyond sequence-based homology detection levels.
source: The extremely sparse phylogenetic distribution of these genes in unicellular eukaryotes, despite our efforts to perform exhaustive searches, has multiple potential explanations. These genes might have been independently lost in many lineages and/or have diverged beyond sequence-based homology detection levels.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for the sparse distribution.

claim: Some GRL homologs might have been acquired by lateral gene transfer.
source: It is also possible that some homologs were acquired by lateral gene transfer, as has been proposed to explain the patchy phylogenetic distribution of microbial rhodopsins (Gavelis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation, supported by analogy to another protein family.

claim: The global conservation of the structural features of unicellular eukaryotic GRLs and DUF3537 proteins with insect chemosensory receptors suggests that they are also ligand-gated ion channels.
source: The global conservation of the structural features of unicellular eukaryotic GRLs and DUF3537 proteins with insect chemosensory receptors suggests that they are also ligand-gated ion channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural similarity.

claim: It is possible, if not likely, that GRL proteins fulfill distinct roles in different phyla.
source: It is possible, if not likely, that the proteins fulfill distinct roles in different phyla, as has been suggested in non-Bilateria, where some GRLs appear to act during development (Saina et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation about functional diversity, supported by citation to developmental roles in non-Bilateria.

claim: In A. thaliana, DUF3537 genes have various tissue-specific expression patterns, including in leaf guard cells, roots and pollen grains.
source: In A. thaliana, transcriptomic analysis indicates that DUF3537 genes have various tissue-specific expression patterns, including in leaf guard cells, roots and pollen grains (Schmid et al., 2005).
evidence: This expression pattern is supported by citation to transcriptomic analysis.

claim: One broadly expressed A. thaliana DUF3537 protein (AT4G22270) localizes to the plasma membrane.
source: For one broadly expressed plant protein (AT4G22270), GFP-tagging revealed localization in the plasma membrane (Guan et al., 2009), and transgenic overexpression appeared to promote organ growth (Guan et al., 2009).
evidence: This localization is supported by citation to a GFP-tagging study.

claim: Transgenic overexpression of AT4G22270 appeared to promote organ growth in A. thaliana.
source: For one broadly expressed plant protein (AT4G22270), GFP-tagging revealed localization in the plasma membrane (Guan et al., 2009), and transgenic overexpression appeared to promote organ growth (Guan et al., 2009).
evidence: This phenotype is supported by citation, but the authors note it requires validation.

claim: The significance of the organ growth phenotype from AT4G22270 overexpression will require validation by loss-of-function genetic analysis.
source: However, the significance of this phenotype will require validation by loss-of-function genetic analysis.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the cited work.

claim: Even if members of the GRL superfamily have a common function as ligand-gated ion channels, they are likely to recognize very diverse chemicals that are potentially of environmental and/or internal origin.
source: Together, the available evidence indicates that even if members of this superfamily have a common function as ligand-gated ion channels, they are likely to recognize very diverse chemicals that are potentially of environmental and/or internal origin.
evidence: This is speculation about ligand diversity based on the functional diversity observed.

claim: The recognition of GRL existence across Animalia, Plantae, Fungi and Protista provides evidence that this protein superfamily originated in the last common eukaryotic ancestor, 1.5–2 billion years ago.
source: While functional studies remain a future challenge, the recognition of their existence across Animalia, Plantae, Fungi and Protista provides evidence that this protein superfamily originated in the last common eukaryotic ancestor, 1.5–2 billion years ago (Hedges et al., 2006).
evidence: This evolutionary conclusion is based on the phylogenetic distribution and supported by citation for the timing.

claim: No sequences bearing resemblance to GRLs were found in Bacteria or Archaea.
source: No sequences bearing resemblance to GRLs were found, so far, in Bacteria or Archaea.
evidence: This is a negative result from the database searches.

claim: The fungal kingdom is thought to be the closest relative to Animalia.
source: The fungal kingdom is thought to be the closest relative to Animalia (Baldauf and Palmer, 1993).
evidence: This phylogenetic relationship is supported by citation.
